A puzzle shows people the triple 2, 4, 6 and says it fits a secret rule; they must guess the rule by proposing their own triples and being told 'fits' or 'doesn't fit'. Most participants guess 'ascending even numbers, each +2' and only ever test triples that fit their own guess (like 8, 10, 12), rarely proposing a triple designed to fail — even though the real rule is simply 'any three ascending numbers.' What cognitive bias does this classic experiment, devised by Peter Wason, demonstrate?

Take any four-digit number that isn't made of all identical digits (e.g. 3524). Arrange its digits to form the largest possible number and the smallest possible number (using leading zeros if needed), then subtract the smaller from the larger. Repeat this process with each new result. Within seven steps, the process will always settle on the exact same fixed number, no matter which starting number you began with. What is that number?
Which is larger: e^π (roughly 2.71828 raised to the power of pi), or π^e (pi raised to the power of roughly 2.71828)?
choices: It's impossible to compare without a calculator

questions.q: A hotel has infinitely many rooms, numbered 1, 2, 3, ..., and every single room is already occupied by a guest. One more guest arrives asking for a room. Can the hotel accommodate them without evicting anyone?
choices: No — every room is full, so there is no room for another guest
No — infinity plus one is undefined, so the question has no answer
Yes, but only if the hotel first builds an extra room
Yes — move the guest in room n to room n+1 for every n, freeing up room 1

questions.q: You're colouring a map so that no two regions sharing a border have the same colour. According to the Four Colour Theorem, what is the minimum number of colours that is always enough for ANY such map, no matter how many regions it has or how they're arranged?
choices: There is no fixed number — it grows with the number of regions
